directAnswer: Pope St. Eugene I, a Roman cleric, was elected in 654 while his predecessor Martin I was still alive in exile, and he reigned until 657. His legates in Constantinople accepted a compromise statement on the wills of Christ, but the Roman clergy and people rejected it and Eugene did not endorse it.

paras: Eugene was a Roman who had served in the Church from his youth, according to the Liber Pontificalis, which describes him as gentle, kind, and generous. After Martin I was carried off to Constantinople, the Roman clergy delayed for more than a year but, under pressure from the emperor, elected Eugene in August 654. Martin, still alive in exile, seems to have accepted the choice. Eugene's position was delicate: the emperor expected him to be more accommodating than his predecessor.

sections.h2: The Roman Clergy Reject a Compromise
paras: Eugene sent legates to Constantinople to restore relations. They agreed to communion with Patriarch Peter, who offered a formula speaking of two wills and also of one will in Christ, an attempt to bridge the opposing positions. When Peter's synodical letter was read in Santa Maria Maggiore in 656, the clergy and people of Rome rejected it so strongly that they would not let Eugene finish Mass until he promised not to accept it.

Constans II was reportedly angered and threatened to deal with Eugene as he had with Martin, but war with the Arabs occupied him. Eugene died on 2 June 657, which is his feast day, and was buried in St. Peter's. Little more is known about him.

keyFacts: Elected while Pope St. Martin I was still alive in exile
Roman clergy and people rejected Patriarch Peter's compromise formula (656)

faqs.question: How could Eugene I be elected while Martin I was alive?
faqs.answer: Martin had been removed by force and exiled, and the Roman clergy, under imperial pressure, elected Eugene in 654. Martin appears to have acquiesced, and Eugene is recognized as a legitimate pope.

faqs.question: Did Eugene I accept Monothelitism?
faqs.answer: No. His legates in Constantinople went along with an ambiguous formula, but when it reached Rome the clergy and people rejected it and Eugene promised not to accept it.
